scope.basis: Proposed course-bound topic groups; one group may require zero, one, or several assets.
scope.completeness: Automated candidate scan of accepted card exports; not a complete manual per-card or handbook image audit. Some matches may be irrelevant; image-only source material omitted from text may be missed.
scope.method: Keyword rules inspect exact card front and back. A heuristic excludes test-administration summaries without a concrete road scenario; exclusions can miss candidates. Related slides and quiz items are same-section fact-ID joins, not validated placements or proof that image-based assessment exists.
scope.source_status: Page and source references are copied as recorded by existing course exports; content, page fidelity, currentness, and rights are not independently verified.

source_registry.interpretation: Registry assessment status as recorded; a HOLD does not by itself settle the separate question of native structural acceptance.

sources.rights_posture: fact-authority candidate only; PDF/text/images not redistributed; no rights clearance claimed

sources.page_number_note: PDF and printed page values are copied directly from the card source_ref; null means unavailable.

asset_policy.signs: Source accurate authoritative sign artwork; verify local applicability and license before use. Do not invent a road sign.
asset_policy.diagrams: Verify the exact state scenario and claims against current official evidence before making diagrams.
asset_policy.handbook_art: Rights to source artwork have not been verified; do not assume reproduction is permitted.
asset_policy.accessibility: Use meaningful alt text and avoid relying on color alone.
asset_policy.cross_state: Shared images require state-specific source verification; no rule equivalence is assumed.

source_cards.front: What should you know about turn-signal uses?
source_cards.back: Use turn signals to announce a turn, a change in direction or a lane change on a road with multiple lanes.

needs.title: Mirrors and vehicle blind spots
needs.matching_method: Automated keyword match on actual card front/back; classification and relevance require human/independent review.

source_cards.front: What should you know about rear mirror view?
source_cards.back: The rear-view mirror should give the driver a clear, unobstructed view behind the vehicle.

source_cards.front: What should you know about mirror adjustment timing?
source_cards.back: Set the mirrors before driving so they provide the best available view beside and behind the vehicle.

source_cards.front: What should you know about inside mirror?
source_cards.back: Aim the interior rear-view mirror to frame the rear window and show traffic behind you.

source_cards.front: What should you know about left mirror adjustment?
source_cards.back: For the left outside mirror, rest your head against the closed driver-side window and adjust until only a small part of the vehicle's left edge remains visible.

source_cards.front: What should you know about right mirror adjustment?
source_cards.back: For the right outside mirror, lean until your head is over the center console, then adjust until the rear edge of your vehicle is barely visible.

source_cards.front: What should you know about outside-mirror viewing area?
source_cards.back: The described outside-mirror adjustment adds twelve to sixteen degrees of view on each side, although the vehicle's sides are no longer visible in a normal mirror glance.

source_cards.front: What should you know about tracking a passing vehicle?
source_cards.back: With the described mirror adjustment, a vehicle behind moves from the inside mirror to an outside mirror, then into the driver's peripheral view.

needs.title: Seat belts and child restraints
needs.matching_method: Automated keyword match on actual card front/back; classification and relevance require human/independent review.

source_cards.front: What should you know about front safety belts?
source_cards.back: An average motor vehicle should have at least two safety belts in its front seat.

source_cards.front: What should you know about air bags and belts?
source_cards.back: Air bags supplement safety belts and work best together with them to reduce the chance of the head or upper body striking the interior in a crash.

source_cards.front: What should you know about Ohio safety-belt requirement?
source_cards.back: Drivers and front-seat riders in most passenger vehicles must wear safety belts on Ohio roads, including vehicles equipped with air bags.

source_cards.front: What should you know about passenger restraints?
source_cards.back: Fasten your own safety belt and check that every passenger uses a safety belt or a child restraint.

source_cards.front: What should you know about drivers under eighteen?
source_cards.back: For a driver younger than eighteen, occupancy cannot exceed the number of originally installed safety belts, and every occupant must wear one.

source_cards.front: What should you know about belt placement?
source_cards.back: Place the safety belt over the body's bony shoulder and hip areas.

source_cards.front: What should you know about shoulder belt placement?
source_cards.back: Wear the shoulder belt over the shoulder and chest with little or no slack, never under an arm or behind the back.

source_cards.front: What should you know about incorrect shoulder belt risk?
source_cards.back: Incorrect shoulder-belt use can cause serious internal injury during a crash.

source_cards.front: What should you know about lap belt placement?
source_cards.back: After fastening, tighten the lap belt so it sits low and snug across the hips.

source_cards.front: What should you know about loose lap belt risk?
source_cards.back: A poorly positioned lap belt can let you slide out during a crash, causing injury or death.

source_cards.front: What should you know about seat adjustment before driving?
source_cards.back: Before moving, position the seat for a clear windshield view, full pedal and steering control, and enough room for air-bag deployment.

source_cards.front: What should you know about head restraint position?
source_cards.back: Position the head restraint against the back of your head, at least as high as your ears, to help prevent whiplash.

source_cards.front: What should you know about younger-driver device restriction?
source_cards.back: Drivers younger than eighteen generally cannot use electronic devices even hands-free while driving, stopped at a traffic light or waiting in a traffic jam, subject to the stated exceptions.

source_cards.front: What should you know about right-of-way meaning?
source_cards.back: Right of way means that a pedestrian or vehicle has priority to proceed over others in a particular setting.

source_cards.front: What should you know about earlier intersection arrival?
source_cards.back: Yield to a driver who is already at an intersection or reached it before you.

source_cards.front: What should you know about left-turn yielding?
source_cards.back: When turning left, yield to drivers approaching in the opposing traffic lane.

source_cards.front: What should you know about simultaneous intersection arrival?
source_cards.back: If two drivers reach a four-way intersection together, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right.

source_cards.front: What should you know about entering from private access?
source_cards.back: When entering a public highway from a driveway or private road, yield to traffic on the highway.

source_cards.front: What should you know about entrance-ramp yielding?
source_cards.back: A driver using an entrance or acceleration ramp must yield to vehicles already on the interstate or limited-access highway.

source_cards.front: What should you know about occupied intersection?
source_cards.back: Yield to pedestrians, bicycle riders and other drivers who remain within the intersection.

source_cards.front: What should you know about public-safety vehicles?
source_cards.back: Yield the right of way to public-safety vehicles such as emergency, police and fire vehicles.

source_cards.front: What should you know about funeral procession priority?
source_cards.back: Yield the right of way to a funeral procession.

source_cards.front: What should you know about steady red light?
source_cards.back: At a red light, stop before the intersection and wait behind the stop line, crosswalk or intersection boundary for green.

source_cards.front: What should you know about steady green light?
source_cards.back: A green light permits cautious travel through an intersection only when the way is clear.

source_cards.front: What should you know about flashing yellow light?
source_cards.back: At a flashing yellow light, reduce speed and proceed carefully, ready to stop for traffic entering the intersection.

source_cards.front: What should you know about flashing red light?
source_cards.back: At flashing red, make a complete stop behind the stop line, crosswalk or intersection, then enter only after checking that no traffic crosses your path.

source_cards.front: What should you know about nonworking signal?
source_cards.back: Treat a traffic light that is not operating like a stop sign, yielding and entering the intersection cautiously.

source_cards.front: What should you know about crosswalk yielding?

source_cards.front: What should you know about pavement marking forms?
source_cards.back: Road markings may take the form of painted lines, arrows, words or symbols.

source_cards.front: What should you know about pavement marking functions?
source_cards.back: Pavement markings divide lanes and identify passing permissions, turn lanes, pedestrian paths and stopping points for signs or signals.

source_cards.front: What should you know about solid yellow centerline?
source_cards.back: A solid yellow line separates traffic moving in opposite directions.

source_cards.front: What should you know about double solid yellow lines?
source_cards.back: Do not cross left of double solid yellow centerlines except to turn left or pass a slow-moving vehicle, such as a bicycle or a vehicle showing a slow-moving-vehicle sign.

source_cards.front: What should you know about dashed side of mixed centerlines?
source_cards.back: Beside a solid-and-dashed yellow centerline pair, drivers on the dashed-line side may pass other vehicles.

source_cards.front: What should you know about solid side of mixed centerlines?
source_cards.back: Beside a solid-and-dashed yellow centerline pair, drivers on the solid-line side may not pass other vehicles.

source_cards.front: What should you know about dashed yellow centerline?
source_cards.back: With a dashed yellow centerline, drivers in either direction may pass vehicles going their way when the maneuver is safe.

source_cards.front: What should you know about two-way turn lane markings?
source_cards.back: A shared two-way left-turn lane has solid and dashed yellow borders on both sides and white arrows indicating left turns from either direction.

source_cards.front: What should you know about stop line before crosswalk?
source_cards.back: Obey a stop line placed before a crosswalk.

source_cards.front: What should you know about crosswalk marking differences?
source_cards.back: Crosswalk markings do not all have the same appearance.

source_cards.front: What should you know about guide-sign services?
source_cards.back: Guide signs can direct travelers to hospitals, fuel or service stations, restaurants and hotels.

source_cards.front: What should you know about approaching a work zone?
source_cards.back: Near a construction area, stay alert, slow down, obey the signs and watch for workers and equipment.

source_cards.front: What should you know about work-zone sudden stops?
source_cards.back: Approaching or traveling through a work zone requires readiness for an unexpected stop.

source_cards.front: What should you know about work-zone following space?
source_cards.back: Keep a clear gap behind the vehicle ahead in a work zone instead of following too closely.

source_cards.front: What should you know about work-zone speeding consequences?
source_cards.back: Speeding in a work zone can result in doubled fines and jail time.

source_cards.front: What should you know about approaching emergency vehicle?
source_cards.back: For an approaching public-safety vehicle using flashing lights and an audible warning, move as far right as possible and remain stopped until it passes, except when it approaches from the opposite side of a divided highway.

source_cards.front: What should you know about turn signaling distance and method?

source_cards.front: What should you know about stop sign or red signal?
source_cards.back: Before entering an intersection at a stop sign or red light, stop behind the stop line or crosswalk.

source_cards.front: What should you know about permitted red-light turn stop?
source_cards.back: Even when a red-light turn is permitted, first stop completely behind the stop line or crosswalk and yield to crossing traffic and pedestrians.

source_cards.front: What should you know about flashing-red priority?
source_cards.back: Stop at a flashing red signal and yield to traffic that is not required to stop.

source_cards.front: What should you know about leaving private access?
source_cards.back: In a business or residential district, stop at the sidewalk when leaving an alley, driveway or private road, or before the roadway if there is no sidewalk, and yield to sidewalk pedestrians.

source_cards.front: What should you know about insufficient room beyond intersection?
source_cards.back: Stop before an intersection when there is not enough space beyond it for your vehicle, even if the signal permits movement.

source_cards.front: What should you know about intersection search?
source_cards.back: At every intersection, slow down and check traffic controls, pedestrians, pavement conditions and places where visibility is limited.

source_cards.front: What should you know about intersection traffic scan?
source_cards.back: Check oncoming and crossing traffic, including motorcycles and bicycles, by looking left, right and left again.

source_cards.front: What should you know about left-turn yielding?
source_cards.back: Yield to oncoming traffic before making a left turn.

source_cards.front: What should you know about left turn at green?
source_cards.back: The handbook directs a left-turning driver at green to wait for a turning opportunity; if heavy traffic prevents one, it describes placing the vehicle's front slightly beyond the stop bar, yielding to pedestrians and opposing traffic, and turning when safe.

source_cards.front: What should you know about right turn at red?
source_cards.back: A right turn at red is allowed unless a sign forbids it, after a complete stop and after all crossing vehicles and pedestrians clear the intersection.

source_cards.front: What should you know about blocked intersection at green?
source_cards.back: Even at green, wait before the intersection until traffic beyond it moves enough to let you clear it without blocking crossing traffic.

source_cards.front: What should you know about restricted view at stop sign?
source_cards.back: After stopping where cross traffic is hidden, edge forward to obtain a view before entering the intersection.

source_cards.front: What should you know about roundabout entry priority?
source_cards.back: Yield to vehicles already circulating before entering a roundabout or traffic circle.

source_cards.front: What should you know about obstruction exception to right-half rule?
source_cards.back: An obstruction may require driving left of center, but the driver must yield to oncoming traffic.

source_cards.front: What should you know about passing exception to right-half rule?
source_cards.back: Passing a vehicle traveling in the same direction is a stated exception to the right-half roadway rule.

source_cards.front: What should you know about roundabout layout?
source_cards.back: In a roundabout or traffic circle, vehicles move counterclockwise around a raised central island.

source_cards.front: What should you know about roundabout approach lane?
source_cards.back: Check direction signs before entering a roundabout because lane changes are not allowed inside it.

source_cards.front: What should you know about roundabout entry speed?

source_cards.front: What should you know about roundabout entry priority?

source_cards.front: What should you know about roundabout entry scan?

source_cards.front: What should you know about roundabout exit signal?

source_cards.front: What should you know about listed roundabout right-turn exit?
source_cards.back: The handbook's listed roundabout pattern uses the first exit for a right turn.

source_cards.front: What should you know about listed roundabout straight exit?

source_cards.front: What should you know about listed roundabout left-turn exit?

source_cards.front: What should you know about listed roundabout reversal exit?
source_cards.back: The handbook's listed roundabout pattern uses the fourth exit to reverse direction with a U-turn.

source_cards.back: For an approaching public-safety vehicle using flashing lights and an audible warning, move as far right as possible and remain stopped until it passes, except when it approaches from the opposite side of a divided highway.

needs.title: Turning lanes and turn paths
needs.matching_method: Automated keyword match on actual card front/back; classification and relevance require human/independent review.

source_cards.front: What should you know about avoiding a wide right turn?
source_cards.back: Do not swing left before making a right turn.

source_cards.front: What should you know about right-turn position?
source_cards.back: Turn right from the far-right part of your lane into the far-right part of the destination street.

source_cards.front: What should you know about left-turn yielding?
source_cards.back: Yield to oncoming traffic before making a left turn.

source_cards.front: What should you know about left-turn lane position?
source_cards.back: Turn left from the far-left part of your lane into the destination lane farthest left but just right of its center divider, including on four-lane highways.

source_cards.front: What should you know about left turn at green?
source_cards.back: The handbook directs a left-turning driver at green to wait for a turning opportunity; if heavy traffic prevents one, it describes placing the vehicle's front slightly beyond the stop bar, yielding to pedestrians and opposing traffic, and turning when safe.

source_cards.front: What should you know about multiple turn lanes?
source_cards.back: Enter the intended turning lane before the turn and remain in that lane until the turn is finished.

source_cards.front: What should you know about right turn at red?
source_cards.back: A right turn at red is allowed unless a sign forbids it, after a complete stop and after all crossing vehicles and pedestrians clear the intersection.

source_cards.front: What should you know about left turn at red street conditions?
source_cards.back: A left turn at red is allowed only from the far-left lane of a one-way street into another one-way street, unless a posted sign prohibits that turn.

source_cards.front: What should you know about listed roundabout right-turn exit?
source_cards.back: The handbook's listed roundabout pattern uses the first exit for a right turn.

source_cards.front: What should you know about listed roundabout left-turn exit?
source_cards.back: The handbook's listed roundabout pattern uses the third exit for a left turn.

source_cards.front: What should you know about listed roundabout reversal exit?
source_cards.back: The handbook's listed roundabout pattern uses the fourth exit to reverse direction with a U-turn.

needs.title: Following distance and stopping distance
needs.matching_method: Automated keyword match on actual card front/back; classification and relevance require human/independent review.

source_cards.front: What should you know about stopping-distance factors?
source_cards.back: Stopping distance depends on reaction time, travel speed, brake condition and pavement condition.

needs.title: Bicycles and cyclists
needs.matching_method: Automated keyword match on actual card front/back; classification and relevance require human/independent review.

source_cards.front: What should you know about double-yellow passing rule?
source_cards.back: On a two-lane two-way road with double solid yellow centerlines, passing is prohibited except for a safe pass of a slow-moving vehicle such as a bicycle or a vehicle with a slow-moving-vehicle sign.

needs.title: Intersections and right of way
needs.matching_method: Automated keyword match on actual card front/back; classification and relevance require human/independent review.

source_cards.front: What should you know about passing at intersections?
source_cards.back: Do not attempt to pass at an intersection.

source_cards.front: What should you know about intersection and crosswalk parking clearance?
source_cards.back: Except when avoiding a traffic conflict or obeying police or traffic-control directions, do not stop, park or stand in an intersection or crosswalk or within twenty feet of either.

needs.title: Lane changes, passing and blind-spot checks
needs.matching_method: Automated keyword match on actual card front/back; classification and relevance require human/independent review.

source_cards.front: What should you know about lane-change search?
source_cards.back: Before changing lanes, check the mirrors and turn your head over the shoulder toward the intended lane to check blind spots.

source_cards.front: What should you know about completing a lane change?
source_cards.back: Adjust speed and steering as you enter the new lane, then cancel the signal.

source_cards.front: What should you know about exit preparation?
source_cards.back: Know the intended exit and move toward its lane early enough to avoid a sudden lane change.

needs.title: Freeway merging, entrances and exits
needs.matching_method: Automated keyword match on actual card front/back; classification and relevance require human/independent review.

source_cards.front: What should you know about freeway merge search?
source_cards.back: On a freeway entrance, watch the vehicle ahead and use an over-shoulder check and outside mirrors to locate a merging gap.

source_cards.front: What should you know about freeway merge speed?
source_cards.back: Signal and accelerate in the entrance lane to the speed of freeway traffic before merging, then cancel the signal.

source_cards.front: What should you know about using an exit lane?
source_cards.back: Maintain speed on the main roadway, signal into the deceleration lane, and slow there while observing its posted speed.

source_cards.front: What should you know about center turn lane restrictions?
source_cards.back: A shared center left-turn lane serves left turns from either direction and must not be used for passing, merging into traffic or through travel.

needs.title: Mirrors and vehicle blind spots

source_cards.front: What should you know about blind spots?
source_cards.back: Blind spots are nearby areas that the interior and outside rear-view mirrors do not show.

source_cards.front: What should you know about lane-change search?
source_cards.back: Before changing lanes, check the mirrors and turn your head over the shoulder toward the intended lane to check blind spots.

source_cards.front: What should you know about freeway merge search?
source_cards.back: On a freeway entrance, watch the vehicle ahead and use an over-shoulder check and outside mirrors to locate a merging gap.

source_cards.front: What should you know about return after passing?
source_cards.back: Continue a pass until both headlights of the passed vehicle appear in the rear-view mirror, then signal and return smoothly while maintaining an appropriate speed.

needs.title: Parking, reversing and maneuvering
needs.matching_method: Automated keyword match on actual card front/back; classification and relevance require human/independent review.

source_cards.front: What should you know about one-way curb parking?
source_cards.back: On a one-way street, parallel parking is allowed within twelve inches of either curb.

needs.title: Parking on hills and wheel position
needs.matching_method: Automated keyword match on actual card front/back; classification and relevance require human/independent review.

source_cards.front: What should you know about hill-parking sequence in the handbook?
source_cards.back: For hill parking, the handbook directs turning the front wheels toward the curb side, selecting park, setting the parking brake and switching off the engine.

needs.title: Parking locations and restrictions
needs.matching_method: Automated keyword match on actual card front/back; classification and relevance require human/independent review.

source_cards.front: What should you know about accessible parking authorization?
source_cards.back: Do not use a wheelchair-marked accessible parking space without an issued removable windshield placard or accessible license plate.

source_cards.front: What should you know about fire hydrant parking clearance?
source_cards.back: Do not stop, park or stand within ten feet of a fire hydrant unless needed to avoid a traffic conflict or to comply with police or traffic-control directions.

source_cards.back: On a two-lane two-way road with double solid yellow centerlines, passing is prohibited except for a safe pass of a slow-moving vehicle such as a bicycle or a vehicle with a slow-moving-vehicle sign.

source_cards.front: What should you know about double-yellow driveway turn?
source_cards.back: A driver may cross double solid yellow centerlines to turn left into a driveway when it is safe.

source_cards.front: What should you know about solid-and-dashed passing side?
source_cards.back: On a two-lane two-way road with a solid-and-dashed yellow centerline, passing is allowed only from the dashed-line side and is prohibited from the solid-line side.

source_cards.front: What should you know about crossbuck-only approach?
source_cards.back: Where only pavement markings or crossbucks mark a crossing, approach slowly and be ready to stop for a train seen or heard.

source_cards.front: What should you know about passing before crossings or bridges?
source_cards.back: Do not attempt a pass before a railroad crossing or bridge.

source_cards.front: What should you know about railroad warning signs?
source_cards.back: Railroad crossings may be identified by a round yellow sign bearing a cross and the letters R R, or by a white crossbuck labeled Railroad Crossing.

source_cards.front: What should you know about railroad active warnings?
source_cards.back: Some railroad crossings have train-activated flashing red lights and may also have a gate.

source_cards.front: What should you know about railroad track obstruction?
source_cards.back: Do not stop a vehicle on railroad tracks or try to cross ahead of an approaching train.

source_cards.front: What should you know about railroad stop sign?
source_cards.back: Every vehicle must stop before proceeding through a railroad crossing marked by a stop sign.

source_cards.back: Railroad crossings may be identified by a round yellow sign bearing a cross and the letters R R, or by a white crossbuck labeled Railroad Crossing.

source_cards.front: What should you know about railroad warning response?
source_cards.back: At a railroad warning sign, slow down and prepare to stop if you see or hear an approaching train.

source_cards.front: What should you know about school-bus red lights?
source_cards.back: When a school bus stops to load or unload children, its amber lights change to four flashing red lights, with two at each end.

source_cards.front: What should you know about school-bus stop arm?
source_cards.back: A school bus may extend a flashing stop arm from its left side, but the absence of that arm does not remove the stopping requirement.

source_cards.front: What should you know about school bus on fewer than four lanes?
source_cards.back: On a road with fewer than four lanes, traffic approaching a stopped school bus from either direction must stop at least ten feet from it until the bus moves or its driver signals permission to proceed.

source_cards.front: What should you know about school bus on four or more lanes?
source_cards.back: On a road with at least four lanes, only traffic going the bus's direction must stop behind a stopped school bus and wait until the bus moves.

source_cards.front: What should you know about cargo-area restraint exception?
source_cards.back: The open-cargo-area restriction has an exception for a properly secured seat and a safety belt meeting federal restraint standards.

source_cards.front: What should you know about child-seat standards and installation?
source_cards.back: Use a child safety seat meeting federal motor-vehicle safety standards, installed properly and used according to its manufacturer's instructions.

source_cards.front: What should you know about rear-facing seat and active air bag?
source_cards.back: Never put a rear-facing child seat in front of an active passenger air bag.

source_cards.front: What should you know about young or light child restraint?
source_cards.back: Children younger than four or weighing less than forty pounds, including those meeting both conditions, need a suitable federally compliant child seat in vehicles subject to the stated restraint law.

source_cards.front: What should you know about child-restraint vehicle exemptions?
source_cards.back: The listed child-restraint exemptions include public-safety vehicles, taxicabs and vehicles that did not legally need safety belts when manufactured.

source_cards.front: What should you know about young riders in open cargo areas?
source_cards.back: A driver must not knowingly carry someone younger than sixteen in an open or unroofed truck, trailer or semitrailer cargo area above twenty-five miles per hour unless a stated exception applies.

source_cards.front: What should you know about fog crash response?
source_cards.back: After a crash in fog, move off the road as soon as it is safe; if the vehicle cannot move, leave lights and flashers on and place flares if possible.

source_cards.front: What should you know about belt during a stop?
source_cards.back: Remain calm and keep the safety belt fastened during a police stop.

source_cards.front: What should you know about responding to a skid?
source_cards.back: If the vehicle skids, release the accelerator, steer in the skid's direction and do not apply the brakes while skidding.

source_cards.front: What should you know about work-zone approach cues?
source_cards.back: On a work-zone approach, watch for signs, cones, barrels, large vehicles and workers.

source_cards.front: What should you know about winter following space?
source_cards.back: Leave more space than usual behind other vehicles because slippery roads increase stopping distance.

needs.matching_method: Automated keyword match on actual card front/back; classification and relevance require human/independent review.

source_cards.front: What should you know about work-zone conditions?
source_cards.back: A work zone is a roadwork area that may include closed lanes, detours and moving equipment.

source_cards.front: What should you know about unoccupied work-zone speed?
source_cards.back: Slow down in a work zone even if no workers are present because narrow lanes and rough pavement can still be hazardous.

source_cards.front: What should you know about vulnerable road-user space?
source_cards.back: Give extra room to pedestrians, particularly children, and to bicycle riders.

source_cards.front: What should you know about horn communication?
source_cards.back: Use a light horn tap to attract attention when pedestrians or cyclists approach your lane, when a vehicle you are passing begins moving into it, or when a driver seems unaware of you.

source_cards.front: What should you know about signal before slowing for a turn?
source_cards.back: Signal before slowing to turn off a road without a separate turn or exit lane, or to park or turn before an intersection.

source_cards.front: What should you know about signaling direction changes?

source_cards.front: What should you know about prolonged side-by-side travel?

source_cards.front: What should you know about slippery-road handling?
source_cards.back: Reduced tire grip on slippery pavement increases stopping distance and makes turning without a skid harder.

source_cards.front: What should you know about hydroplaning meaning?
source_cards.back: Hydroplaning happens when the steering tires ride over pooled water instead of gripping the roadway.

source_cards.front: What should you know about hydroplaning prevention?
source_cards.back: Slow down in rain and on wet roads containing pooled water or puddles to reduce hydroplaning traction loss.

source_cards.front: What should you know about hydroplaning response?
source_cards.back: If hydroplaning occurs, ease off the accelerator slowly.

source_cards.front: What should you know about extra space behind large vehicles?
source_cards.back: Increase the following gap behind trucks, buses, recreational vehicles and vehicles towing trailers.

source_cards.front: What should you know about space beside a passing tractor-trailer?
source_cards.back: As a tractor-trailer passes, move toward the outer part of your own lane to leave a little more clearance from it.

source_cards.front: What should you know about space cushion?
source_cards.back: A space cushion is the gap kept between your vehicle and other road users that gives you time to respond.

source_cards.front: What should you know about stopping distance meaning?
source_cards.back: Stopping distance covers the vehicle's movement from recognizing a need to stop until the vehicle is stationary under ideal conditions.

source_cards.front: What should you know about speed and stopping distance?
source_cards.back: Higher travel speed requires more time and distance to stop.

source_cards.front: What should you know about braking distance example?
source_cards.back: At fifty miles per hour on dry pavement with good brakes, the handbook gives about one hundred fifty-eight feet as a possible braking distance.

source_cards.front: What should you know about extra space on slippery roads?
source_cards.back: Increase the following distance on slippery pavement.

source_cards.front: What should you know about bicycle traffic direction?
source_cards.back: A bicycle on the roadway is a vehicle and must travel with other traffic rather than against it.

source_cards.front: What should you know about bicycle road duties?
source_cards.back: Bicycle riders must obey signs, signals and pavement markings and follow the same road rules as motorized traffic.

source_cards.front: What should you know about approaching a bicycle?
source_cards.back: Reduce speed when approaching or passing a bicycle rider.

source_cards.front: What should you know about horn near a bicycle?
source_cards.back: Avoid sounding the horn close to a bicycle rider.

source_cards.front: What should you know about safe bicycle passing?
source_cards.back: Pass a bicycle only when the maneuver can be completed safely.

source_cards.front: What should you know about bicycle clearance?
source_cards.back: Keep at least three feet between a motor vehicle and a bicycle.

source_cards.front: What should you know about turning near a bicycle?
source_cards.back: Do not turn sharply across a bicycle rider's path or force the rider off the road.

source_cards.front: What should you know about bicycles on poor surfaces?
source_cards.back: Use particular care around bicycles on wet, sandy or gravel-covered roads because these conditions affect them more than motor vehicles.

source_cards.front: What should you know about bicycle search before backing?
source_cards.back: Check for bicycle riders in the vehicle's path before backing.

source_cards.front: What should you know about bicycle rider intention clues?
source_cards.back: Learn bicycle arm signals and, if a rider cannot signal, look for clues such as a head turn or shoulder check before a lane change.

source_cards.front: What should you know about motorcyclist rights?
source_cards.back: Motorcycle riders have the same roadway rights and duties as other drivers, although they can be harder to see.

source_cards.front: What should you know about motorcycle lane space?
source_cards.back: Give a motorcycle the full width of its lane so its rider has room to respond to other traffic.

source_cards.front: What should you know about searching for motorcycles?
source_cards.back: Include motorcycles in mirror and blind-spot checks.

source_cards.front: What should you know about motorcycle stopping statement?
source_cards.back: The handbook states that motorcycles require more stopping distance than cars and other passenger vehicles.

source_cards.front: What should you know about motorcycle turn-signal caution?
source_cards.back: Do not assume a motorcycle will turn merely because its signal flashes, since the signal may not cancel automatically and may have been left on.

source_cards.front: What should you know about motorcycle ideal following gap?
source_cards.back: At low speed in ideal conditions, keep at least three seconds behind a motorcycle.

source_cards.front: What should you know about motorcycle expanded following gap?
source_cards.back: Use at least four seconds behind a motorcycle with higher speeds, heavy traffic, poor visibility, bad weather, unfamiliar surroundings or driver fatigue.

source_cards.front: What should you know about motorcycle hazard maneuvers?
source_cards.back: Expect a motorcyclist to change speed or lane position suddenly to avoid potholes, gravel, slippery surfaces, pavement seams, rails or grooved pavement.

source_cards.front: What should you know about inside a turning truck?

source_cards.front: What should you know about stop lines and truck turning space?

source_cards.front: What should you know about cutting off a truck?
source_cards.back: Do not cut in front of a large vehicle to reach a turn or exit or to enter a single-lane work zone ahead of it.

source_cards.front: What should you know about no-zone locations?
source_cards.back: A truck's or bus's no-zones are blind areas beside it, behind it and in front of it, with larger trucks having larger blind areas.

source_cards.front: What should you know about large-vehicle side visibility?
source_cards.back: The handbook warns that if you cannot see a truck or bus driver's face in the outside mirror, that driver cannot see you.

source_cards.front: What should you know about travel beside a large vehicle?

source_cards.front: What should you know about loaded-truck stopping example?
source_cards.back: In ideal conditions, a loaded truck with good tires and adjusted brakes traveling fifty-five miles per hour needs at least three hundred thirty-five feet to stop.

source_cards.front: What should you know about truck stopping comparison?
source_cards.back: The handbook's loaded-truck example is more than one and a half times the stopping distance of a passenger vehicle.

source_cards.front: What should you know about returning ahead of a truck?
source_cards.back: Before moving back in front of a passed large vehicle, see its entire front in the rear-view mirror and maintain speed.

source_cards.front: What should you know about large-vehicle rear blind area?
source_cards.back: A large vehicle's rear blind area can extend as far as two hundred feet behind it.

source_cards.front: What should you know about following a large vehicle?
source_cards.back: Do not follow a large vehicle closely; position your vehicle where its driver can see you in an outside mirror and where your own forward view is not blocked.

source_cards.front: What should you know about truck areas on hills and near scales?
source_cards.back: Avoid the right lane behind a large vehicle on steep climbs or descents and near truck weigh stations where trucks may rejoin faster traffic.

source_cards.front: What should you know about breakdown position?
source_cards.back: When a vehicle breaks down, move it off the road and away from traffic if possible.

source_cards.front: What should you know about breakdown warning lights?
source_cards.back: Activate emergency flashers to warn that the vehicle is disabled.

source_cards.front: What should you know about breakdown flares?
source_cards.back: If possible, place emergency flares about two hundred to three hundred feet behind a broken-down vehicle to warn approaching drivers.

source_cards.front: What should you know about waiting after breakdown?
source_cards.back: The handbook instructs occupants to stay in the vehicle until assistance arrives after a breakdown.

source_cards.front: What should you know about moving after a crash?
source_cards.back: After a crash, move the vehicle as far off the roadway as possible; if it cannot move, activate hazards and place available road flares.

source_cards.front: What should you know about nonworking signals and police directions?
source_cards.back: Treat an inoperative traffic signal as a four-way stop unless a law-enforcement officer is directing traffic, and proceed carefully because others may fail to stop.

source_cards.front: What should you know about anti-lock braking information?
source_cards.back: Most newer vehicles have anti-lock braking intended to prevent skidding during a stop; consult the vehicle manual for the proper braking method.

source_cards.front: What should you know about skid causes?
source_cards.back: Excessive speed for conditions, an abrupt stop or loss of tire grip can cause a skid.

source_cards.front: What should you know about initial skid response?
source_cards.back: At the start of a skid, release pressure on the brake or accelerator and steer into the skid.

source_cards.front: What should you know about parking brake after brake failure?
source_cards.back: If normal brakes fail, apply the parking brake slowly so the rear wheels do not lock and cause a skid.
